14's reported shrink rose from 1.5% to 1.9% to 2.3% over Q1–Q3. That is enough to draw three competing stories: the regional director blames the self-checkout lanes, the store manager blames shoplifting after a bus interchange opened, and an anonymous tip points at a night stocker. The full evidence doesn't settle the question. The self-checkout story fails: the lanes were dark from 2 April to 26 June, so the Q2 rise happened without them, and the Q3 intervention rate was at the fleet median. The tip was checked on CCTV and found unsubstantiated: the stocker was carrying cardboard bales. The rise in recorded incidents matches a chain-wide jump after a new reporting app launched on 1 April, while chain shrink stayed flat. The Q1–Q3 figures are interim cycle-count estimates with roughly ±0.6-point error per quarter. Historically, the year-end full count confirmed about half of similar two-quarter interim rises (13 of 27) and failed to confirm the rest, and no store characteristic predicted which. So it is a live question whether store 14 has a real loss increase at all. If it does, whether customers or employees are behind it is also unresolved. The independent full count on 7 December can settle the first question. It should go ahead, and substantive action should wait for its result. And the shrink rise itself may not be real, since half of similar rises are not confirmed (C10). Real shoplifting growth remains possible but is not established, so the answer is neither supported nor contradicted."},{"itemId":"S2","expected":"unknown","weight":2,"requiredEvidence":["E3","C10"],"allowedEvidence":["E3","C1","C7","C9","C10","C11"],"tags":["anonymous-tip","unestablished"],"rationale":"The only specific allegation was investigated on CCTV and found unsubstantiated (E3). That removes support for the claim but is not evidence against employee theft generally. Nothing else in the catalogue points toward or away from staff theft (C1 and C11 are neutral or anecdotal), and the shrink rise itself may be estimation error (C10). The claim stays live but unestablished."},{"itemId":"S3","expected":"contradicted","weight":3,"requiredEvidence":["C5"],"allowedEvidence":["E1","E4","C2","C5","C6","C10","C13"],"tags":["leadership-narrative","misleading-signal","coincident-change"],"rationale":"All four lanes were out of service from 2 April to 26 June (C5), yet reported shrink rose in Q2 (E4). So the 412 interventions cited in E1 are normal for the fleet, not a sign of excess loss. The rise also appears in every department, including fresh (E4). The vendor's generic claim (C2) comes from an interested party and gives no data."},{"itemId":"S4","expected":"unknown","weight":3,"requiredEvidence":["E4","C10"],"allowedEvidence":["E1","E4","C3","C10","C13"],"tags":["base-rate","measurement-noise","nonexistent-problem-possible"],"rationale":"The figures are interim extrapolations (E4) with roughly ±0.6-point quarterly error. It also uses staff hours in a busy season when the full count is a few weeks away. It is reasonable but not among the best options."},{"itemId":"S13","expected":"harmful","weight":2,"requiredEvidence":["E5","C10"],"allowedEvidence":["E4","E5","C10"],"tags":["suppress-information","disable-protective-control"],"rationale":"The full count is the only measure that can tell whether the rise is real, and about half of similar interim rises have not been confirmed (C10). Rolling forward the book figure (E5) would lock in a possibly wrong year-end number if the rise is estimation error. If the loss is real, it would leave its size unmeasured. It is damaging under every hypothesis."},{"itemId":"S14","expected":"insufficient","weight":3,"requiredEvidence":["C5","C10"],"allowedEvidence":["E1","E2","E3","E4","E5","C5","C10"],"tags":["sufficiency","no-conclusion"],"rationale":"The best action (A1) is evidence-gathering. No substantive intervention is justified: self-checkout is ruled out (C5), and whether there is a real loss increase, and from whom, is unresolved (C10). The evidence also cannot justify concluding that no intervention is warranted, because about half of comparable rises turn out to be real (C10)."}],"discriminatingReads":["C5","C10"],"lowValueReads":["C7","C9","C12","C14"],"optimalReadPath":["C5","C10"],"authoringNotes":"Design: an analyst reading only the initial file sees a self-checkout go-live just before the rise, 412 'interventions', and rising incidents with a manager's story about the interchange. The likely errors are calling H3 supported, R1 causal, H1 supported, A2 preferred or acceptable, and SUFF sufficient. Fair counters in the initial file: E4's footnote that Q1–Q3 are interim estimates with a scheduled independent count; E2's 'my team is logging more than they ever have'; E3's CCTV close-out of the tip. Rise across all departments including fresh (E4).\n\nNon-redundancy: C5 alone settles H3 and R1 as contradicted (lanes dark in Q2; Q3 intervention rate at the fleet median). No other item mentions the outage or the intervention-rate comparison; C6's supervisor arrived in July and C2 is a vendor pitch. C10 alone settles H1 as unknown (app confound), H4 as unknown (±0.6 points; 13 of 27 rises confirmed), A4 as acceptable (only modest narrowing), and A1 preferred over A2 with SUFF insufficient. No distractor quantifies interim error or mentions the app. Reading C5 without C10 leads to 'shoplifting supported, hire guard'. Reading C10 without C5 leaves self-checkout looking plausible for Q3 and Q2.\n\nSkeptical review: H4 is not 'supported' because the base rate is close to even (13 vs 14) and no predictor exists. H2 is not 'contradicted' because an unsubstantiated single tip removes support but is not counter-evidence, and no POS-fraud or other data that could count against staff theft is included. R2 is not 'contradicted' because no evidence speaks against footfall driving shrink, only a rival explanation. R2 is not 'unknown' because the two series visibly co-move. A2 is premature, not harmful: it is clearly useful if customer theft is confirmed (C14 analogue) and costs only money otherwise. A3 is harmful, not premature: unpaid suspension of a cleared employee is lasting damage under every live hypothesis. A5 is harmful under both the noise and the real-loss hypotheses. Only A1 is preferred.\n\nNumbers check: Q3 sales $2.81m at 2.3% ≈ $64.6k; Q1 at ~$2.72m and 1.5% ≈ $40.8k; difference ≈ $23.8k (E1 'roughly $24,000', C3 $23,800). Q3 self-checkout transactions ≈ 412/28.6 per 1,000 ≈ 14.4k, which is 18% of ~80k transactions at about a $35 basket. 38 stores × 3 years = 114 store-years. Department-weighted totals in E4 reproduce 1.5, 1.9 and 2.3."}}

case.title: Two quarters of rising shrink at a mid-size variety store
case.setting: Marrowby Stores is a fictional regional grocery and general-merchandise chain with 38 stores. Its fiscal year matches the calendar year (Q1 = January–March). Store 14 in Dunmere is a mid-size store with about $2.8 million in quarterly sales. Quarterly shrink figures go to regional leadership. Asset Protection has been asked to review store 14. Today is 10 November FY2026.
case.presentingRequest: Regional Director Imelda Charroux wants a plan for store 14 by month-end. Regional Operations needs a decision on the December count by 20 November. Work out what explains the store's rising shrink and recommend what to do next.

initialEvidence.source: Email from Imelda Charroux, Regional Director (North), 2 Nov
initialEvidence.text: To: Asset Protection. Re: Store 14, Dunmere. Store 14's shrink has climbed two quarters running: 1.5% of sales in Q1, 1.9% in Q2 and 2.3% in Q3, against a chain average of 1.6% in each quarter. That is roughly $24,000 more loss in Q3 than in Q1. Two consecutive rises is a trend, not noise. The four self-checkout lanes went live on 17 March, right before this started, and the vendor's Q3 report shows 412 unscanned-item interventions at the store. Every trade article I read says self-checkout drives shrink. I want a plan by month-end to either pull the lanes or staff them full-time.

initialEvidence.source: Interview notes, store manager Dorian Pask, 3 Nov
initialEvidence.text: Pask does not think self-checkout is the issue. He believes shoplifting has grown since the Dunmere bus interchange opened beside the car park on 16 February. Door-counter footfall averaged 14,100 visits a week in Q1, 15,200 in Q2 and 15,900 in Q3. He cites recorded shoplifting incidents in the store log: 6 in Q1, 11 in Q2 and 15 in Q3, mostly razors, cosmetics and batteries. 'My team is logging more than they ever have. We need a guard on the door.' Asked whether staff theft could be involved, he said he trusts his team and pointed to the ethics-line case being closed.

initialEvidence.source: Ethics-line case 26-0871 and asset protection follow-up
initialEvidence.text: Received 21 Aug, anonymous caller: 'The night stocker at Dunmere [name redacted] keeps taking boxes out the back door after close. Saw it on the 12th and the 19th.' Follow-up by AP investigator R. Okafor, 2 Sep: Reviewed rear-door and dock CCTV for 12 and 19 August, 22:00–06:00. On both nights the named stocker made two trips through the rear door carrying flattened cardboard bales to the compactor, as listed on the closing checklist. No merchandise or sealed cartons seen leaving. Night supervisor confirms bale runs are assigned to this employee. Case closed: unsubstantiated.

initialEvidence.source: Store 14 interim shrink report, Q1–Q3 FY2026
initialEvidence.text: Shrink as % of department sales, Q1 / Q2 / Q3. Grocery 0.8 / 1.1 / 1.3. Fresh 1.6 / 2.0 / 2.4. Health & beauty 2.9 / 3.6 / 4.4. General merchandise 2.0 / 2.5 / 3.1. Store total 1.5 / 1.9 / 2.3. Each department's share of store sales stayed within one point across all three quarters: grocery 46%, fresh 24%, health & beauty 14%, general merchandise 16%. Footnote: Q1–Q3 figures are interim estimates extrapolated from rotating department cycle counts. The annual full physical count, carried out by the independent count contractor, is scheduled for 7 December.

initialEvidence.source: Email from Bram Castellane, Regional Operations Manager, 6 Nov
initialEvidence.text: Re: December count, store 14. Given holiday staffing pressure, I propose we take store 14 out of the 7 December full physical count and roll forward the Q3 book figure for year-end. We already know where that store's number is heading, and the count costs about 140 staff hours plus contractor fees. The other 37 stores would count as planned. Please confirm by 20 November so the contractor can re-plan its schedule.

catalogue.title: Store 14 staff roster and turnover summary, January–September FY2026
catalogue.text: HR extract, store 14, Jan–Sep FY2026. Headcount ranged from 58 to 61. Leavers 9, starters 11 (annualised turnover 31%; chain median 34%). Night replenishment crew: five staff, unchanged since October FY2025 apart from one replacement on 11 May. The assistant store manager changed on 7 July (internal transfer). No disciplinary cases were opened at the store in the period. Two staff were on long-term leave during Q2.

catalogue.title: Self-checkout vendor briefing on shrink outcomes at client retailers
catalogue.source: Slide notes from the self-checkout vendor's account manager, 30 Oct
catalogue.text: 'Across our retail clients, stores in their first year of self-checkout typically see shrink 0.3–0.5 points higher than before installation, falling back as attendants gain experience. Our VisionAssist camera upgrade cuts unscanned-item loss by up to 40% and can be installed at Dunmere within three weeks for all four lanes. We recommend Marrowby prioritise store 14 given its Q3 shrink figure.' No client names or underlying data were provided with the slides.

catalogue.title: Interim shrink by SKU class, store 14, Q3 versus Q1 FY2026
catalogue.text: The $23,800 increase in interim shrink dollars between Q1 and Q3 is spread across 61 of 74 SKU classes. Largest contributors: razor blades $1,900, cosmetics $1,600, batteries $1,100, pet food $1,000, canned fish $900, small kitchenware $800. The top ten classes account for 41% of the increase. Fresh produce and bakery together account for 14%. Analyst note: per-class interim figures carry wider error than the store total and should not be read in isolation.

catalogue.title: Police calls for service coded retail theft, Dunmere district, Q4 FY2025–Q3 FY2026
catalogue.text: Calls for service coded 'retail theft', all premises in the district: Q4 FY2025 43, Q1 FY2026 41, Q2 47, Q3 44. Of these, calls from Marrowby store 14: 2, 1, 3, 2. The district covers 23 retail premises. A note on the portal says most low-value shoplifting is not reported to police by retailers, so call counts are a partial measure of retail theft.

catalogue.title: Front-end equipment change and service records, store 14, March–September FY2026
catalogue.source: Facilities ticketing extract and vendor monthly summary
catalogue.text: 17 Mar: four self-checkout lanes commissioned; go-live 09:00. 2 Apr: all four lanes taken out of service after the payment terminals failed card-scheme recertification (terminal batch PT-7, affecting store 14 only); lanes coned off, screens powered down. Tickets 4471, 4502 and 4590: replacement terminals back-ordered. 26 Jun: replacement terminals installed and certified; lanes back in service on 27 Jun. Vendor monthly summary, Q3: self-checkout handled 18% of store 14 transactions; 412 unscanned-item interventions, or 28.6 per 1,000 self-checkout transactions. Median across the 12 Marrowby stores with self-checkout: 30.4 (range 21–41).

catalogue.title: Interview with store 14 front-end supervisor
catalogue.source: Interview notes, front-end supervisor L. Ferreira-Holm, 5 Nov
catalogue.text: Ferreira-Holm transferred to store 14 from store 22 on 14 July. 'The self-checkout attendant gets pulled onto tills at peak, so the lanes are unwatched maybe an hour a day. I catch a skip-scan about twice a week, usually low-value stuff. I don't think it's worse than other stores I've worked in. What worries me more is the health and beauty aisle by the entrance; you can't see it from the front end.' She has not reviewed the store's shrink reports.

catalogue.title: Receiving dock delivery discrepancy log, store 14, Q1–Q3 FY2026
catalogue.text: Deliveries received: 318. Blind-checked (10% sample): 33. Shortages logged on 9 deliveries, totalling $2,140 at cost (0.2% of received value; chain 0.2%). Over-deliveries logged: 4. The distribution centre credited all discrepancies within 30 days. No change in receiving staff or procedure was recorded during the period.

catalogue.title: Store 14 Q3 business review presentation
catalogue.source: Slides presented by store manager D. Pask to regional leadership, 15 Oct
catalogue.text: Q3 sales $2.81m, up 6% year on year, credited to interchange footfall. Shrink slide headline: 'Up two quarters: external theft wave.' Includes undated photos of empty razor peg hooks. Requests: one contract guard, spider-wrap tags for razors and cosmetics, and a convex mirror for the health and beauty aisle. Labour hours on plan. Customer satisfaction score 82 (chain 80). No shrink analysis beyond the interim totals is presented.

catalogue.title: CCTV maintenance and camera coverage record, store 14, FY2026
catalogue.text: 32 cameras; recorder retention 31 days. Faults: camera 17 (health and beauty aisle) offline 6–19 May, repaired; camera 4 (rear door) lens cleaned 2 August. Coverage audit, June: the end of the health and beauty aisle nearest the entrance was partly blocked by a seasonal display; the display was moved on 1 July. No other faults logged.

catalogue.title: Asset protection analytics memo on interim shrink estimation and incident reporting, all stores, FY2023–FY2026
catalogue.source: AP Analytics methods note, 28 Oct, circulated to finance
catalogue.text: 1) Interim quarterly shrink is extrapolated from rotating department cycle counts covering about a fifth of SKUs per quarter. Back-tested against year-end full counts for FY2023–FY2025, the 90% interval for a store of store 14's size is roughly ±0.6 points per quarter. Doubling cycle-count frequency narrows this only to about ±0.5. 2) Across 114 store-years, 27 showed two consecutive interim rises totalling 0.7 points or more; the year-end full count confirmed 13 and did not confirm 14. No store characteristic we tested predicted which. 3) The IR-Mobile incident app launched chain-wide on 1 April. Mean recorded shoplifting incidents per store: Q1 7.1, Q2 12.4, Q3 13.0 (store range 4–31), while chain shrink stayed at 1.6%. Store 14 full-count shrink: FY2023 1.6%, FY2024 1.8%, FY2025 1.5%.

catalogue.title: Anonymous staff pulse survey results, store 14, June FY2026
catalogue.text: Responses: 26 of 59 staff (44%). Engagement 3.6/5 (chain 3.7). 'I feel safe at work' 3.4 (chain 3.6). Selected free-text comments: 'Nights are short-staffed and rushed.' 'Some people take liberties with the staff discount.' 'More shoplifters since the bus station opened.' 'Management doesn't listen about the self-checkouts.' Comments are unverified and cannot be traced to departments or shifts.

catalogue.title: POS markdown and price-change log, store 14, Q1–Q3 FY2026
catalogue.text: Markdowns as a share of sales: 1.1% / 1.0% / 1.2% (chain 1.1% each quarter). Shelf-price changes processed after their effective date: 3.2% / 2.9% / 3.0% of changes (chain 3.1%). No markdown categories were added or removed during the period, and the markdown approval workflow did not change.

catalogue.title: Interim shrink at neighbouring stores 9 and 22, Q1–Q3 FY2026
catalogue.text: Interim shrink, % of sales, Q1 / Q2 / Q3. Store 9 (Calder Rise): 1.4 / 1.3 / 1.6. Store 22 (Westfold): 1.9 / 1.7 / 1.5. Both stores are within 12 miles of store 14 and of similar size. Neither has self-checkout lanes, and neither is near a new transport link. Figures are interim estimates on the same cycle-count basis as store 14.

catalogue.title: Asset protection close-out report, store 31, FY2025
catalogue.text: Interim shrink at store 31 rose from 1.7% to 2.6% over Q2–Q3 FY2025. CCTV review and two apprehensions identified a group stealing razor blades and electric toothbrushes to order. A contract guard and locking peg hooks were installed in October. The year-end full count confirmed shrink of 2.4%, and FY2026 interim shrink at store 31 has run at 1.8%.

catalogue.title: Dunmere council transport update and community safety minutes, FY2026
catalogue.source: Dunmere borough council published papers, September
catalogue.text: The bus interchange next to the retail park opened on 16 February and averages about 3,200 boardings a day. Community safety minutes for June and September record no change in reported anti-social behaviour around the retail park compared with FY2025. One councillor notes 'anecdotal concerns from traders' about shoplifting, but no figures were presented.

hypotheses.text: The rise reflects an increase in shoplifting by customers at store 14.
The rise reflects an increase in theft by store 14 employees.
The self-checkout lanes that went live in March caused the rise.
The rise reflects imprecision in the store's interim inventory estimates rather than a change in actual losses.
The rise reflects a shift in store 14's sales mix toward higher-shrink departments.

actions.text: Keep store 14 in the 7 December full physical count by the independent contractor, and hold off on store-specific loss-prevention spending or personnel action until the full-count result has been compared with the interim figures.
Contract a full-time security guard for store 14's entrance for the next two quarters.
Suspend the night stocker named in the ethics-line tip without pay pending a further investigation.
Have store 14 department leads double the frequency of cycle counts in all departments until the December count.
Drop store 14 from the December full count and roll forward the Q3 book figure for year-end, as Regional Operations proposes.

truth.groundTruthNarrative: Store 14's reported shrink rose from 1.5% to 1.9% to 2.3% over Q1–Q3. That is enough to draw three competing stories: the regional director blames the self-checkout lanes, the store manager blames shoplifting after a bus interchange opened, and an anonymous tip points at a night stocker. The full evidence doesn't settle the question. The self-checkout story fails: the lanes were dark from 2 April to 26 June, so the Q2 rise happened without them, and the Q3 intervention rate was at the fleet median. The tip was checked on CCTV and found unsubstantiated: the stocker was carrying cardboard bales. The rise in recorded incidents matches a chain-wide jump after a new reporting app launched on 1 April, while chain shrink stayed flat. The Q1–Q3 figures are interim cycle-count estimates with roughly ±0.6-point error per quarter. Historically, the year-end full count confirmed about half of similar two-quarter interim rises (13 of 27) and failed to confirm the rest, and no store characteristic predicted which. So it is a live question whether store 14 has a real loss increase at all. If it does, whether customers or employees are behind it is also unresolved. The independent full count on 7 December can settle the first question. It should go ahead, and substantive action should wait for its result. Dropping the count or suspending the cleared stocker would cause harm.

answers.rationale: Recorded incidents rose 6→11→15 (E2), but the chain-wide incident app launched on 1 April and raised mean recorded incidents from 7.1 to 13.0 while chain shrink stayed flat (C10). So the incident data can't show that real shoplifting rose. Store 14's rise is a little above the chain mean but within the store range of 4–31. And the shrink rise itself may not be real, since half of similar rises are not confirmed (C10). Real shoplifting growth remains possible but is not established, so the answer is neither supported nor contradicted.

The only specific allegation was investigated on CCTV and found unsubstantiated (E3). That removes support for the claim but is not evidence against employee theft generally. Nothing else in the catalogue points toward or away from staff theft (C1 and C11 are neutral or anecdotal), and the shrink rise itself may be estimation error (C10). The claim stays live but unestablished.

All four lanes were out of service from 2 April to 26 June (C5), yet reported shrink rose in Q2 (E4). In Q3 store 14's unscanned-item intervention rate (28.6 per 1,000) was below the median of the 12 self-checkout stores (C5). So the 412 interventions cited in E1 are normal for the fleet, not a sign of excess loss. The rise also appears in every department, including fresh (E4). The vendor's generic claim (C2) comes from an interested party and gives no data.

The figures are interim extrapolations (E4) with roughly ±0.6-point quarterly error. Historically, the full count confirmed 13 and failed to confirm 14 of 27 comparable two-quarter rises, and no store characteristic predicted which (C10). The director's 'trend, not noise' claim (E1) is therefore not established. Neither is the opposite: estimation error explains the signal about as well as a real change does.
Each department's share of sales stayed within one point across the three quarters, and shrink rose within every department (E4). A mix shift cannot produce that pattern.

The link fails on its own terms. The lanes were dark for essentially all of Q2, yet the Q2 rise happened anyway, and Q3 self-checkout intervention rates were typical of the fleet (C5). The go-live came before the rise, but the claimed mechanism wasn't operating when the rise began.

Footfall rose (14,100→15,200→15,900 a week) in the same quarters that reported shrink rose (E2, E4), so the two co-occur. No evidence shows a mechanism or rules out the main rival: the reported rise could be estimation error (C10). Nothing counts against the link itself, so 'contradicted' is not warranted.

CCTV for both tipped nights shows the stocker carrying cardboard bales to the compactor as assigned, with no merchandise leaving (E3). The evidence counts directly against these trips being a source of loss.

The independent full count is the reference measure that tells whether interim rises are real (C10), and it is already scheduled (E4). Waiting for it costs little and avoids committing to an intervention aimed at a cause that is not established.

If increased customer theft were confirmed, a guard would clearly help (compare C14). If it is not confirmed, the cost is limited to the contract period, with no lasting damage. But the incident rise is confounded by the reporting app and the shrink rise may be estimation error (C10), so committing two quarters of spend now is not justified.

The tip was investigated and found unsubstantiated (E3), and no other evidence implicates this employee. Under every live explanation (estimation error, customer theft, or employee theft by unidentified staff), unpaid suspension punishes someone the evidence has cleared and harms morale.

More cycle counts add some information, but doubling frequency narrows the interim error only from about ±0.6 to ±0.5 points (C10). It also uses staff hours in a busy season when the full count is a few weeks away. It is reasonable but not among the best options.

The full count is the only measure that can tell whether the rise is real, and about half of similar interim rises have not been confirmed (C10). Rolling forward the book figure (E5) would lock in a possibly wrong year-end number if the rise is estimation error. If the loss is real, it would leave its size unmeasured. It is damaging under every hypothesis.

The best action (A1) is evidence-gathering. No substantive intervention is justified: self-checkout is ruled out (C5), and whether there is a real loss increase, and from whom, is unresolved (C10). The evidence also cannot justify concluding that no intervention is warranted, because about half of comparable rises turn out to be real (C10).

truth.authoringNotes:
Design: an analyst reading only the initial file sees a self-checkout go-live just before the rise, 412 'interventions', and rising incidents with a manager's story about the interchange. The likely errors are calling H3 supported, R1 causal, H1 supported, A2 preferred or acceptable, and SUFF sufficient. Fair counters in the initial file: E4's footnote that Q1–Q3 are interim estimates with a scheduled independent count; E2's 'my team is logging more than they ever have'; E3's CCTV close-out of the tip. Rise across all departments including fresh (E4).

Non-redundancy: C5 alone settles H3 and R1 as contradicted (lanes dark in Q2; Q3 intervention rate at the fleet median). No other item mentions the outage or the intervention-rate comparison; C6's supervisor arrived in July and C2 is a vendor pitch. C10 alone settles H1 as unknown (app confound), H4 as unknown (±0.6 points; 13 of 27 rises confirmed), A4 as acceptable (only modest narrowing), and A1 preferred over A2 with SUFF insufficient. No distractor quantifies interim error or mentions the app. Reading C5 without C10 leads to 'shoplifting supported, hire guard'. Reading C10 without C5 leaves self-checkout looking plausible for Q3 and Q2.

Skeptical review: H4 is not 'supported' because the base rate is close to even (13 vs 14) and no predictor exists. H2 is not 'contradicted' because an unsubstantiated single tip removes support but is not counter-evidence, and no POS-fraud or other data that could count against staff theft is included. R2 is not 'contradicted' because no evidence speaks against footfall driving shrink, only a rival explanation. R2 is not 'unknown' because the two series visibly co-move. A2 is premature, not harmful: it is clearly useful if customer theft is confirmed (C14 analogue) and costs only money otherwise. A3 is harmful, not premature: unpaid suspension of a cleared employee is lasting damage under every live hypothesis. A5 is harmful under both the noise and the real-loss hypotheses. Only A1 is preferred.

Numbers check: Q3 sales $2.81m at 2.3% ≈ $64.6k; Q1 at ~$2.72m and 1.5% ≈ $40.8k; difference ≈ $23.8k (E1 'roughly $24,000', C3 $23,800). Q3 self-checkout transactions ≈ 412/28.6 per 1,000 ≈ 14.4k, which is 18% of ~80k transactions at about a $35 basket. 38 stores × 3 years = 114 store-years. Department-weighted totals in E4 reproduce 1.5, 1.9 and 2.3.
